 Galectin-3 Restricts Dengue Virus Infection Through Envelope Binding and Immune Signaling
 by 
 November 15, 2026 
 in 
 Biology 
 Reading Time: 3 mins read
 0 
 Galectin-3 Restricts Dengue Virus Infection Through Envelope Binding and Immune Signaling
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 The host protein galectin-3 restricts dengue virus serotype 2 infection by directly binding to the viral envelope glycoprotein, inhibiting viral entry, and enhancing pro-inflammatory NF-κB signaling pathways, according to laboratory and animal findings reported in Virology Journal. Currently, no antiviral therapy is approved for dengue virus, an important pathogen whose pathogenesis remains a major challenge. Galectin-3 is a recognized β-galactoside-binding lectin known to modulate several distinct viral infections, yet its precise mechanistic role in dengue virus infection and disease development had not been previously established.
 To systematically determine how this lectin influences viral replication, the research team employed a green fluorescent protein-tagged DENV-2 reporter virus across multiple cellular experimental conditions. The investigators evaluated the biological consequences of administering purified recombinant galectin-3, depleting cellular protein levels through targeted knockdown, and increasing cellular protein abundance through experimental overexpression. In addition to assessing replication kinetics, the authors analyzed specific steps in the viral life cycle, focusing on initial viral attachment to host cells and subsequent viral internalization.
 Initial cellular observations revealed that active DENV-2 infection led to a marked down-regulation of endogenous galectin-3 expression within host cells. When the researchers introduced recombinant galectin-3 into the extracellular environment, the protein caused a dose-dependent reduction in both DENV-2 infectivity and the production of infectious progeny virus. A comparable inhibitory outcome was observed when cells were treated with conditioned medium containing naturally secreted galectin-3, demonstrating that extracellular forms of the lectin exert antiviral activity against the virus.
 The inhibitory effect of galectin-3 proved to be highly specific and dependent on defined carbohydrate recognition mechanisms. The antiviral restriction exerted by the protein was effectively reversed by the addition of lactose, a known competitive carbohydrate ligand, as well as by the galectin-3-neutralizing monoclonal antibody B2C10. Conversely, neither the control carbohydrate sucrose nor non-specific control immunoglobulin G reversed the observed viral inhibition, confirming that the protective effect relies on specific glycan binding mediated by the lectin.
 Biochemical and molecular evaluations demonstrated that galectin-3 physically binds the dengue virus envelope glycoprotein, directly hindering both viral attachment and viral internalization into target cells. To clarify the structural basis of this interaction, computational in silico molecular docking was performed against the viral envelope protein. The docking simulations showed that galectin-3 is compatible with engaging both known envelope glycosylation sites, with aggregate computational binding scores favoring interaction at the asparagine-67 (Asn67) glycosylation site.
 Genetic manipulation of endogenous galectin-3 levels further corroborated its protective role during intracellular infection. Experimental knockdown of endogenous galectin-3 significantly enhanced DENV-2 replication, whereas the overexpression of galectin-3 successfully suppressed viral replication. Concurrently, galectin-3 amplified intracellular NF-κB activation and increased the downstream expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically interleukin-6, interleukin-8, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and interleukin-1-beta, notably doing so without altering transcripts for type I interferons.
 To determine whether these in vitro antiviral mechanisms translate into protection within a living organism, the researchers assessed disease outcomes in neonatal galectin-3 knockout mice inoculated intracerebrally with DENV-2. Mice lacking galectin-3 exhibited significantly earlier mortality, carried elevated viral loads within brain tissues, and suffered more severe neuropathology compared to wild-type control animals. These animal results confirmed that endogenous galectin-3 deficiency substantially worsens disease progression and neuropathology in vivo.
 Together, these findings indicate that galectin-3 restricts dengue virus serotype 2 by binding envelope glycans to block entry and by promoting NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory responses. Because galectin-3 deficiency exacerbates infection severity in animal models, the study highlights the lectin as a potential host-directed therapeutic target against dengue virus. However, because these evaluations were conducted in cell culture systems and intracerebrally inoculated neonatal mice, further investigation is required before inferring clinical efficacy or therapeutic utility in human dengue patients.
